title: Recommendations
goals: Apply eligibility requirements before ranking candidates by preferences
Explain a recommendation using its actual scoring rule and limits
Interpret feedback in the context of what was shown and distinguish clicks from satisfaction
vocabulary: Whether an item meets the requirements for consideration
A desired feature used to rank eligible choices
A suggested option produced under a stated process
An opportunity for a person to see an item
A process in which earlier recommendations influence the feedback used for later recommendations

worked_example.title: Read feedback without inventing a motive

rows: The reader noticed or liked it
Reader said J was too long
A stated reason in this context

blocks.text: A click can reflect interest, curiosity or a mistaken tap. No click can reflect a missed display, lack of time or a decision not to choose it. Preserve the observed event separately from any interpretation. More direct feedback may clarify a reason, but one response still describes one person and occasion.

Useful feedback records name the item, what was shown, the system version, the event and any stated reason. Use only information needed for the task. Our paper exercises use invented feedback; they do not require accounts or recording classmates’ browsing behaviour.

guided_practice.title: Explain a recommendation honestly
guided_practice.prompt: Write an explanation of why J was recommended that mentions one preference it does not match. A marketer adds guaranteed enjoyment. Explain why that phrase is unsupported.
guided_practice.answer: J is available in English and its space topic earns 2, the highest score among eligible choices; it is prose rather than the preferred comic. The rule supplies a ranking, not evidence guaranteeing enjoyment.

independent_case.title: Transfer the process to activities
independent_case.task: A fictional learner needs an indoor activity lasting at most 20 minutes. Preferences score 2 for drawing and 1 for solo. Candidates: A drawing, solo, outdoor, 10 minutes; B drawing, group, indoor, 20 minutes; C music, solo, indoor, 15 minutes; D drawing, group, indoor, 18 minutes. Filter, score and return all highest scorers. Only B is then shown and selected; C and D are not shown. State what the feedback establishes and what remains unknown.
independent_case.answer: A excluded because outdoor. B eligible scores 2; C eligible scores 1; D eligible scores 2. Return B and D. Exactly 20 minutes passes at most 20. The log establishes B shown and selected, not enjoyment. Preferences about unshown C and D are unknown; selecting B does not prove rejection of D or validate the choice to hide it.
independent_case.source: primary source W4, first curriculum occurrence

misconceptions: A high score can cancel a failed requirement
Filter on requirements before ranking preferences.
It is an interaction; motive and satisfaction need further evidence.
No clicks means dislike even without exposure
An unseen option has not received a meaningful opportunity for a response.

Return no verified eligible option and explain exclusions or missing facts.

PROCESS  score and rank candidates with chosen tradeoffs
OUTPUT  ordered recommendations plus reasons
CORE IDEA  A recommender ranks possibilities using goals, information, and tradeoffs.

UNDER THE HOOD  Recommendation is ranking, not merely classification. An objective combines relevance signals and constraints; tradeoffs may include familiarity, diversity, novelty, safety, and availability. The top score reflects the objective, not universal quality.

A closer explanation

blocks.title: Requirements come before preference scores
blocks.caption: BookRec1 recommends J from this candidate set. L and M match both preferences but fail a requirement. The recommendation does not guarantee that the reader will enjoy J.

blocks.text: J passes both requirements and scores 2. K passes and scores 1. L fails the English requirement; M fails availability. Do not place L or M above J because they would earn 3 preference points. They are excluded before the eligible scores are compared.

A faithful explanation says J is available in English and has the highest eligible score because its space topic matches the stated preference. It should also mention that J is prose, not comic. Claiming that the system knows the reader will love J would go beyond the computation and the evidence.

blocks.text: CASE 1 — Reader A  Clue: likes survival and long books. Meaning: rank adventure higher.
CASE 2 — Reader B  Clue: wants short humor. Meaning: rank comedy higher.
CASE 3 — Same score  Clue: two books tie. Meaning: need tie policy.
CASE 4 — Unavailable book  Clue: high relevance but unusable. Meaning: constraint changes rank.
BOUNDARY  A recommendation optimizes chosen goals and data; it does not discover what a person truly wants.
Which two pictures are easiest to confuse? What evidence separates them?
